newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia upper house approves 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia upper house approves 1997 budget.

text.p: Russia's 1997 compromise budget passed one more hurdle on Wednesday when the upper house of parliament approved the plans by an overwhelming majority.
But analysts said the government would have its work cut out to meet the targets, which include bringing in revenues of a steep 434 trillion roubles ($76.8 billion).

"It is obvious they are not going to collect the whole 434 trillion roubles, but they will probably come closer to it this year than they did in previous years," said Christopher Granville, chief economist with United City Bank.
"But there will be no glory days in the sense that Russia is actually fulfilling the budget law as passed until until the whole tax system is changed, and that means a new tax code."
The code has been drafted but it is stalled in the lower house of parliament and cannot come into effect before 1998.
The budget, which must now be signed into law by President Boris Yeltsin, envisages a deficit of 3.5 percent of gross domestic product, by Russian calculations.
Approval of the budget -- by 125 votes to 25 -- should help Moscow press its case with the International Monetary Fund, which is backing reforms with a $10 billion three-year loan.
The IMF released two tranches of the loan last week, signalling its approval of Russian economic developments by freeing up funds frozen last year.
Officials had said later tranches of the loan could only be released after the budget was in place.
Finance Minister Alexander Livshits had appealed to deputies to vote for the budget, describing the plan as a realistic one which could not be radically improved.

"On behalf of the government I ask you to support the budget. It will be difficult to fulfil it, but the past six months of work have shown that it is impossible to improve the plan radically," he said.
Livshits said the budget would help keep inflation from rising, reduce yields on government securities and promote economic growth.
Industrial output crept 0.3 percent above year-ago levels last month and gross domestic product rose a slim 0.1 percent.
Livshits said changes in tax legislation could bring the government extra revenue, including some 20 trillion roubles from the taxation of government securities.
New arrangements for excise on oil and gas and tougher controls of alcohol production would bring in another 10.7 trillion roubles, he said.

First Deputy Central Bank Chairman Sergei Aleskashenko told Reuters Financial Television on Wednesday that foreign investors would not be affected by a new 15 percent profits tax on government securities due to double-taxation treaties and the central bank was controlling the situation on financial markets.
He said he expected domestic yields to ease soon to the level of Russia's dollar-denominated Eurobond.

Yields on GKO Treasury bills, which once paid almost 200 percent -- and offered the highest real interest rates in the world -- have fallen sharply in line with inflation and are now around 27 percent.
